title: Bank of America Pilots Zelle-UPI Bridge to Speed NRI Remittances to India
excerpt: Bank of America and Early Warning Services are piloting a link between the US instant-payment network Zelle and India's UPI, promising faster, cheaper remittances for NRIs — though the service is not yet publicly available.
body:
• Bank of America is working with Early Warning Services, Zelle's network operator, on a pilot that would connect the US instant-payment system with India's UPI network.
  • The bridge is aimed squarely at remittances, letting NRIs send money to India through the familiar Zelle interface rather than separate wire or app-based services.
  • The project is still in its pilot stage and is not yet available to the public; no launch timeline has been announced.
  • The move fits India's broader push to take UPI global — the system is now active in 11 countries — and Zelle's own plan to expand into India before the end of this year.

Bank of America is piloting a payments bridge that would connect Zelle, the dominant US peer-to-peer transfer system, with India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI), in a move that could reshape how millions of NRIs send money home.

The bank is working with Early Warning Services, the network operator behind Zelle, on the pilot, according to reports this week. The project aims to let users initiate cross-border transfers through the familiar Zelle experience — potentially the same in-app flow Americans already use for domestic transfers — with funds settling through UPI's rails on the Indian side.

"The India-US corridor is one of the largest remittance flows in the world, and even small improvements in cost and speed compound across billions of dollars."

How the two systems fit together

Zelle and UPI are close cousins in concept but different in architecture. UPI, built by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), processes transfers through standalone mobile apps and third-party interfaces. Zelle, by contrast, is integrated directly into the mobile banking apps of participating US banks. Early Warning Services, Zelle's operator, is owned by seven of America's largest financial institutions: Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank, and Wells Fargo.

That ownership structure gives the pilot real weight. A Zelle-UPI link originating at Bank of America could, if opened to the other owner banks, reach a large share of US retail banking customers quickly.

Context & Background

The pilot lands at a moment when both sides of the corridor are expanding aggressively. Earlier this year Zelle said it would expand services to India — its first overseas market — with initial availability expected before the end of this year. The company framed the move around remittances: "As the world's largest recipient of remittances, India is a natural starting point and an important corridor for the millions of American consumers who regularly send money to the country."

Zelle also unveiled ZelleUSD (ZLUSD), a US dollar-backed stablecoin intended to support its future international payment capabilities in other markets.

On the Indian side, the government and NPCI have spent years internationalising UPI. NRIs can already link international mobile numbers from 12 countries — including the US — to NRE and NRO accounts and transact on UPI apps. UPI's acceptance network now spans 11 countries, and PhonePe's recent UAE central bank licence made it the first Indian app authorised for a foreign foray.

Impact & Analysis

For NRIs in the US, the appeal is straightforward: faster transfers, lower costs, and better transparency than the patchwork of wire services, fintech apps, and SWIFT transfers most remitters rely on today. The India-US corridor is one of the largest remittance flows in the world, and even small improvements in cost and speed compound across billions of dollars.

The competitive dynamics are worth watching too. Cross-border fintechs like Wise, Remitly, and Western Union's digital arm have built businesses on this corridor; a bank-native Zelle-to-UPI channel could undercut them on convenience if the economics hold. The pilot also signals a shift in how US banks view instant cross-border payments — a space where stablecoin-based settlement, via ZLUSD, may eventually play a role.

For now, though, the usual caveats apply: the project is in its pilot stage, pricing and limits are undisclosed, and regulatory approvals on both sides — including the RBI and US banking regulators — will shape what the final product looks like.

Diaspora Angle

Millions of Indian professionals in the US send money to family in India every month. A native Zelle-UPI option would let them do it without leaving their banking app, entering separate credentials, or tracking a third-party transfer — a quality-of-life upgrade that matters precisely because remitting is such a routine chore.

What's Next

Watch for a formal announcement from Bank of America or Early Warning Services on the pilot's scope, timeline, and whether the other six Zelle owner banks will participate. India's payments establishment will also be watching: if the bridge works, NPCI has a template to replicate with other US banks — and other corridors.
